topic: Robert Zajonc (1968): Flashed Nonsense Words & Chinese Symbols — Why Mere Repetition Breeds Affection Without Memory!
visual_mode_reason: Robert B. Zajonc's landmark 1968 Monograph — flashing fake Turkish words ('iktitaf', 'afworbu'), Chinese-style ideographs, and yearbook faces 0 to 25 times so people rated the 25x items as 'good/virtuous/likable' even when flashed at 1–5 ms WITHOUT conscious recognition (Kunst-Wilson & Zajonc 1980)! — pairs crisp visual tachistoscope staging with primary visual cortex perceptual fluency and amygdala habituation.

primary_case.title: Robert B. Zajonc's 1968 University of Michigan 'Attitudinal Effects of Mere Exposure' Experiments (and 1980 Subliminal Polygon Proof)
primary_case.place: Research Center for Group Dynamics, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

people.name: Robert B. Zajonc (pronounced 'Zie-unts')
people.role: Warsaw wartime survivor turned University of Michigan psychologist who proved 'Preferences Need No Inferences' — familiarity breeds warmth BEFORE conscious thought.

people.name: Michigan Undergraduate Volunteers
people.role: Students exposed 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, or 25 times to nonsense Turkish words, Chinese-like characters, and strangers' photographs — consistently liking higher-frequency items best

people.name: William Kunst-Wilson, Richard Moreland & Theodore Mita
people.role: Co-investigators who proved Mere Exposure works at **1-millisecond subliminal flashes** with 50% chance recognition (1980; Moreland & Zajonc 1979) AND explains why you prefer your **mirror image** while friends prefer your **true photo** (Mita, Dermer & Knight 1977).

core_facts.fact: Folk proverbs contradicted each other — *'Familiarity breeds contempt'* vs *'Absence makes the heart grow fonder'* — until **1968 (*Journal of Personality and Social Psychology Monograph Supplement*)**, when University of Michigan psychologist **Robert Zajonc** tested **pure, unrewarded repetition ('Mere Exposure')** across four completely different domains.

First, Zajonc checked **natural language frequencies**: across cultures and languages, **more frequently used words** ('good', 'happy', 'clean', low numbers like 1 and 2) are overwhelmingly rated **more positive** than rare counterparts ('bad', 'sad', 'dirty').

Second, to strip away prior meaning, Zajonc showed Michigan students **12 fake 'Turkish' nonsense words** (*iktitaf, saricik, biwonjni, afworbu, jandara...*) **0, 1, 2, 5, 10, or 25 times** for 2 seconds each, then asked what they *guessed* each word meant on a Good–Bad scale: words seen **25 times** were rated **dramatically 'Good/Positive'** (~4.5+) while **0-exposure words** sat down below **3.0**.

Third and fourth, Zajonc repeated the exact **0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 25 exposure curve** with **12 Chinese-style calligraphic characters** AND **12 Michigan State senior yearbook men's faces** — and in **every single experiment**, liking climbed in a crisp **logarithmic curve** with exposure count.

Even wilder (**Moreland & Zajonc 1979, SRC2; Kunst-Wilson & Zajonc 1980 *Science***): flash irregular polygons for **1 millisecond** so fast that volunteers score **dead-even 50% coin-flip chance** on *'Which shape did you see before?'* — yet when asked *'Which shape do you **LIKE** better?'*, they pick the previously flashed polygon **~60% of the time**. Even **MORE** remarkably, subliminal mere exposure is often **stronger** than conscious exposure.

Look at the **Mirror-vs-Photo everyday stunner** (Mita, Dermer & Knight 1977): show people two versions of their own face — **True Camera Orientation** vs **Mirror-Flipped Orientation** — and **68% of people prefer the Mirror-Flipped version** (the face THEY see every morning brushing their teeth!), while **their romantic partners and close friends prefer the True Camera Orientation** (the face THEY see across the table every day).

Crucial boundary critique (**Burgess & Sales 1971, SRC3; Bornstein 1989 meta-analysis of 208 studies**): (1) if a stimulus starts out **actively unpleasant or disgusting**, repeating it makes people **hate it MORE**, not less; and (2) relentless **homogeneous massed repetition** (>20–50 back-to-back exposures of a simple jingle) eventually hits an **inverted-U boredom dip**.

Neurobiologically, repeated safe encounters **sharpen and speed up encoding in primary visual cortex ('perceptual fluency')** while **quieting novelty-vigilance firing in the amygdala** — and your brain reads that smooth, effortless processing speed as a warm glow of safety and liking.
Developmental and consumer mere-exposure replications show that 8 to 10 spaced non-aversive exposures reliably elevate hedonic liking ratings before satiation plateaus set in.

wow_facts.fact: Show college students completely made-up words like ***iktitaf*** and ***afworbu*** **25 times** vs **0 times**, then ask *'Does this Turkish word mean something wonderful or something awful?'* — whichever random nonsense word got the **25 flashes** is confidently judged to mean **something wonderful**.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Pure repetition manufactured positive meaning out of thin air.

wow_facts.fact: Ever wonder why **you hate how you look in group photos** while your friends say *'You look totally normal!'*? Because your mirror flips your asymmetric face left-to-right every morning — Mere Exposure makes **you** love your mirror face (68%) and makes **your friends** love your real unflipped face.
wow_facts.why_surprising: The best cocktail-party demonstration of Mere Exposure ever discovered.

wow_facts.fact: Flash polygons for **one-thousandth of a second (1 ms)**: subjects score **50% pure guesswork** at recognizing which shapes appeared, yet reliably **PREFER** the old shapes anyway — prompting Zajonc's immortal line: ***'Preferences need no inferences!'***
wow_facts.why_surprising: Your heart warms up to familiarity before conscious memory even knows it's met.

misconceptions.myth: 'Familiarity breeds contempt' — seeing something often naturally makes people dislike it.
misconceptions.truth: Across 208 experiments (Bornstein 1989), neutral and mildly pleasant stimuli grow **more liked** with distributed exposure; contempt only arises when an initially *noxious* experience is forced repeatedly or over-played without spacing.

misconceptions.myth: People have to consciously remember an ad, logo, or song for repetition to build brand warmth.
misconceptions.truth: Moreland & Zajonc (SRC2) and Kunst-Wilson & Zajonc (1980) proved exposure boosts affective liking **even at 0% above-chance conscious recognition** — indeed, conscious awareness of ad bombardment can actually dampen the boost.

misconceptions.myth: A radical new product design, song melody, or habit should feel 'amazing at Sight #1' or be scrapped.
misconceptions.truth: Because novel patterns start with low perceptual fluency and mild amygdala vigilance, innovative songs and designs almost always climb sharply between **Exposure 1 and Exposure 10**.

everyday_hooks: Hating a new song on your favorite artist's album on Listen #1 — then humming it as your favorite track by Listen #7.
Cringing at your unflipped smartphone back-camera photo because you've seen your **mirror-reversed face** 10,000 mornings in the bathroom.
Stopping yourself from mistaking **mere media repetition** of a slogan or rumor for truth or virtue ('illusory truth' cousin of mere exposure!).
